name: Philemon
author: The letter comes from the apostle Paul, a Jewish teacher who had once persecuted Christians before becoming one of the best-known travelling missionaries of the early church. Almost all scholars agree that Paul wrote it. He wrote while held as a prisoner, probably under guard and awaiting trial. His younger co-worker Timothy is named alongside him.
audience: The letter is addressed mainly to Philemon, a believer of some means, most likely living in Colossae, a small town in what is now western Turkey. It concerns Onesimus, a slave from Philemon's household who had left him, met Paul, and become a Christian. Most think Onesimus had run away, though some suggest he went to Paul for help in a dispute with his master.
era: This was the Roman Empire of the mid-first century AD, where slavery was an ordinary part of life and a runaway slave could face harsh punishment. Christians were still a small movement with no church buildings, gathering in private homes. Traditionally Paul wrote from house arrest in Rome around AD 60–62, under the emperor Nero. Some scholars suggest an earlier imprisonment in Ephesus, nearer Colossae, in the mid-50s.

notes.1:1: Besides Philemon, the greeting names Apphia and Archippus, probably members of his household, and the church that met in his home, so the letter was likely read aloud there.
notes.1:8: The name Onesimus meant "useful", a common slave name, and Paul plays on it; Onesimus was likely travelling back carrying this letter, possibly with Paul's helper Tychicus.
notes.1:17: Letters were usually dictated to a scribe, so Paul writing a line in his own hand made his promise to repay any loss a personally signed pledge.
notes.1:22: Paul expected to be released soon; the companions he names, including Epaphras, Mark and Luke, also appear in Colossians, linking the two letters.
